title: Why do small businesses still not have bank loans? Is it the firm, the loan price, or the bank? Guest post by Emma Zhang

Why do small businesses still not have bank loans? Is it the firm, the loan price, or the bank? Guest post by Emma Zhang

Development Impact Guest Blogger

November 06, 2026

This page in:

English

English

This is the second in this year’s job market series.
Increasing access to bank loans for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in low- and middle-income countries is considered vital for economic development. Interventions to boost SME lending exist in most countries, and they are commonly implemented through commercial banks as partial default guarantees or loans with promotional interest rates. These two interventions are widespread even in countries where the fewest SMEs have bank loans, yet the percentage of registered firms that apply in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains lower than anticipated.
Many would declare that promotional interest rates need to be pushed even lower. However, interpreting the low number of applications as low demand for loans could be a mistake for three reasons. First, in countries where credit information is scarce, SMEs cannot submit their own applications—loan officers need to spend time gathering information on the prospective borrowers under the guidance of the bank’s underwriting team. Second, loan officers report hesitations to screen many prospective SME borrowers after initial discussions, because SMEs are unwilling to discuss how their financial statements were generated and struggle to acknowledge their business’s industry and idiosyncratic risks. Third, offering promotional loans is the loan officer’s decision. Banks can always lend at whatever interest rates they deem appropriate, meaning that internally, promotional lending schemes are a way for banks to incentivize loan officers to offer lower interest rates to certain borrowers. Lending interventions might offer incentives for commercial bank head offices to want to lend, but these incentives might not translate into benefits for loan officers. Taken together, low applications might be driven by firms never having arrived at the bank, by firms being unable to secure acceptable loan terms, or by the loan officer denying them. Firms that the bank would want to consider for promotional loans might not be asking for them, or loan officers might not be properly incentivized to offer. Critically, these nuances would not be captured in bank administrative data, as the first time firms appear is when applications are submitted.
In my job market paper, we study what drives the low number of application submissions for small business bank loans in Pakistan, where all small business bank loans to new borrowers are partially guaranteed against default by the central bank, and every commercial bank has lending schemes advertising lower-than-market interest rates for small business borrowers.
We do this by recruiting 702 firms across Pakistan, referring them to loan officers, and documenting where they drop out of the application process. Along the way, we randomize two interventions to firms: (i) information on the existence of lending schemes at commercial banks (“Every registered SME was eligible to be considered for a 9%, physical-collateral free loan under the State Bank of Pakistan’s Asaan Finance Scheme”), and (2) preparation for the first meeting with loan officers (via a mock interview, specific feedback, and quick tips).
Registered SMEs in our experiment were recruited via the Small Medium Enterprise Development Authority of Pakistan, local trade bodies, and local commerce chambers. Respondents were told the study was about how SMEs in Pakistan finance themselves, and relative to the average SME, they were more likely to have audited financial statements and accept digital payments from customers. Over 90% of the firms were in manufacturing or services (IT, software, accounting, education) and less than 10% were in retail.
How far do firms make it? Do they drop out before or after they arrive at the bank?
We find very little aversion to the bank, as measured by 80% firms requesting a referral to the bank and by 51% having a real interaction with a loan officer. Instead, we find the main point of dropoff to occur after interacting, but before advancing to the screening stage of the application process, where loan officers visit the business and regenerate parts of the accounting statements from transaction level data to verify validity.
We find that of the SME-loan officer pairs that interacted but did not result in applications, 63% explicitly said that interest rate or collateral stopped the process, and 27% said more generally that the SME was no longer interested. Taken together, this means that 90% of dropoff was driven by SMEs giving up on the bank loan, and not by loan officer denials. 

What about promotional interest rates? Were they still too expensive, or were loan officers not offering?
The average interest rate was 11% in the control group, and 51% were asked for land or property collateral. 25% of the control group received a 9% interest rate or lower.
We find that loan officers were not offering promotional loans, which regardless of scheme, have lower interest rates than standard rates. SMEs that received information on the 9% interest scheme and were eligible to be considered by the bank were actually 8pp (33%) less likely to receive a 9% quote from a loan officer, and they were asked for 2pp (19%) more interest. We find that this result was not driven by SMEs receiving favorable collateral terms or loan sizes, this was not driven by scheme information being interpreted as a signal of low firm quality, and this was not driven by scheme information increasing the animosity of negotiations or changing the observed or expected interaction time between SME and loan officer pairs.
Additional to the information treatment effect on interest, we also find that firms randomly referred to SME loan officers who reported having greater default-concerns were 19pp (88%) more likely to be quoted a high interest, land or property-collateralized loan, which is the most expensive type. More default-concerned loan officers were also not more likely to screen prospective borrowers in the experiment.
This increase in loan price by default concern goes against two common notions of how academics typically think banks should want loan officers to behave. First, we assume that banks include default penalties as part of loan officer compensation because it should increase efforts to verify borrower quality. In our experiment, it seems like default penalties pushed loan officers to lesson efforts to lend, and the commission and bonuses paid to loan officers for lending were not sufficient. Second, we assume banks credit ration, meaning they prefer loan officers to deny prospective borrowers they do not want to lend to instead of raising the interest rates. This is because raising interest rates increases default rates. In our experiment, it seems like default penalties may have adversely selected the sample of borrowers willing to proceed in the application process.
Taken together, our results suggest that loan officers are not incentivized to offer promotional loans over standard ones, and that the interest rates offered under standard loans might have been pushed higher than the bank would have preferred due to the current design of loan officer default penalties.

Policy implications
While a firm that does not apply for a bank loan does not receive one, the distinction between loan officers intentionally pricing out firms and directly denying firms matters for banking regulation, as allowing loan prices to rise without regulation is considered undesirable for financial system stability. Higher interest rates can induce adverse selection, excessive risk-taking, and strategic default. Higher interest rates can also be considered predatory and can destroy trust in the financial system. These are among the reasons why the State Bank of Pakistan constrains the interest rates banks charge to small business borrowers, although this is implemented after applications are submitted as the full distribution of offered interest rates is not easily observed.
These findings also matter beyond Pakistan. The World Bank has made mobilizing private capital a central pillar of its jobs strategy, and we should hope that capital reaches small businesses through domestic banks. Our study highlights why targeting banks with interventions might not necessarily translate into supporting SMEs.
Our study suggests several directions for future research regarding SME bank lending in LMICs. The first is understanding how to better support SMEs through the loan negotiation and screening process. The second is understanding how to adjust organizational incentives for loan officers to support the disbursement of promotional loans. The third is investigating how loan officer default penalties can be redesigned to encourage screening and lending rather than higher interest rate quotes.
Emma Zhang is a PhD student at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business.
